summary: Explains how to decode facsimile data coming from the Rapicom 450 fax machine. It is a companion to the memo describing that machine's file format.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how to turn Rapicom 450 fax data into a bitmap. It describes how blocks identify valid bits and how coded black-and-white pixel pairs are rebuilt.

questions: how do you decode rapicom 450 fax data
subtitle: How to decode Rapicom 450 facsimile data into a bitmap.

tldr.problem: Rapicom 450 fax data uses block framing, reversed bits, and a two-dimensional run-length code, so a decoder must interpret several layers correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the file interface, the block header, four column states, run-length fields, and the procedure for rebuilding scan lines as a bitmap.
tldr.outcome: The decoded bitmap can be displayed or edited using other tools. The memo is an implementation description for this fax format.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 798's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC documents decoding for the Rapicom 450 format.

sections.title: From Fax Data to a Bitmap
sections.content:
The memo describes a program that reads Rapicom 450 facsimile data and decodes it into an ordinary bitmap. The program could then display the image on another device or edit it and encode it back into the Rapicom format.

The fax connects through a microprocessor interface called FAXIE. Data arrives serially in octets, most-significant bit first; the interface complements the bits, and the stored file format also requires bit-order handling described in the RFC and RFC 769.
sections.plainLanguage: The decoder reads the fax machine's coded data and reconstructs a black-and-white bitmap. It must reverse the transformations used by the interface and file format.

sections.title: Blocks and Their Headers
sections.content:
Each fax data block contains 585 bits: a 24-bit synchronization code, a 37-bit header, 512 data bits, and a 12-bit CRC checksum. Only the number of data bits named in the header is useful; the rest are ignored. A block can end partway through a scan line.

The header gives a cycling sequence number, flags, useful-data count, horizontal position, black and white run-word sizes, and starting state. Many fields are sent in reverse bit order, but the sequence number and state are not. The X position tells the decoder where the block's pixels belong and whether gaps or overlaps must be handled.
sections.plainLanguage: Every block has a marker, instructions, image data, and an error-check value. Its header says how much data to use and where that data belongs on the scan line.

sections.title: Rebuilding the Scan Lines
sections.content:
The encoding handles two scan lines at a time. Each column is one of four states: white-white, white-black, black-white, or black-black. Bit patterns move between states. In the all-white and all-black states, variable-length run words represent repeated columns; the word size can change as a run continues.

The decoder starts each block using the state and horizontal position in its header, then reads transitions and reverses the run fields as specified. If a sequence number shows a missing block, or a bit pattern has no valid transition, the decoder can discard bad data or resume at a later block. It continues until the end command or available data ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The decoder tracks whether each pair of pixels is black or white. Short codes mark changes, while run lengths stand for repeated columns, letting it rebuild the image line by line.
